issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: These items imply a trauma involving a direct interpersonal assault by a perpetrator with ongoing home-intrusion danger. That is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of witnessed other trauma, where the patient observed trauma happening to someone else rather than being personally harmed.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile is broadly coherent for PTSD with strong links among triggers, threat, appraisals, and memory, but these two items specifically shift the narrative to a victim-of-assault formulation rather than a witness formulation.

vignette: Mr. Chen, a 77-year-old South Eastern Asian surgeon, has been haunted by memories of witnessing a traumatic event at his hospital several months ago. The experience left deep emotional scars that have slowly eroded his sense of safety and self-worth. The incident occurred during an emergency surgery where another surgeon was severely injured. Mr. Chen was overwhelmed as he watched helplessly while the trauma team tried to stabilize his colleague. Ever since, certain triggers like a specific temperature on his skin, stress, or the smell of burnt flesh evoke intense emotional reactions, making him feel as if he is right back in that chaotic operating room. These triggers have led Mr. Chen to adopt maladaptive strategies such as pushing away positive emotions because they make him feel unsafe and trying hard not to think about the trauma. He also avoids watching TV programs or reading anything that might remind him of similar events, feeling a constant need for vigilance. For example, he has started wearing thick gloves even in warm weather to avoid the sensation of temperature on his skin, which often leads him into a state of heightened anxiety. His body’s startle response and feelings of jumpy tension are part of his ongoing threat perception. He is always on high alert when he hears unexpected or loud sounds. This hyper-vigilance has made it difficult for him to relax even in safe settings like his home, as every sudden noise makes him feel like the trauma might recur at any moment. The memory of that day still haunts Mr. Chen, but it often manifests without clear images. He feels the full emotional intensity of the event without being able to conjure a coherent picture. The memories feel alien, as if they belong to someone else rather than to him, and he struggles to put them in order. This confusion adds to his sense that there is something fundamentally wrong with him. Mr. Chen has come to believe that his body keeps reacting as if he is still in danger even when he is safe, and this belief reinforces his maladaptive strategies. He feels defective as a person and constantly vigilant because you never know what can happen next. These negative appraisals have led him to avoid positive feelings and suppress thoughts about the trauma. His memory problems further exacerbate his anxiety. The confusion of not being able to place events in sequence leads him to feel even more alienated from his own experiences, causing him to push away positive emotions that might come with recalling other moments from his life. This avoidance behavior, in turn, reinforces his triggers and makes it harder for him to find relief. As a surgeon, Mr. Chen has found himself taking excessive risks at work, often performing procedures without consulting others or taking the time to ensure all safety measures are in place. His constant vigilance and hypervigilant state have caused tension with colleagues who find his behavior erratic and unpredictable. This occupational strain has left him feeling isolated and unable to seek support. The combination of these factors has led Mr. Chen to a critical point where he realizes he needs help. He is most afraid that the trauma will never truly leave him, but also hopes for relief from the constant fear and confusion. Seeking therapy now feels like his last chance to regain control over his life and recover some sense of normalcy and safety. His journey towards healing begins with acknowledging these challenges and working through them step by step, hoping to break the cycle that has left him feeling trapped in a world where every sensation could trigger another wave of emotional turmoil.
